clinicalPearls: A rare primary cutaneous mucinosis characterised by dermal deposition of mucin rich in hyaluronic acid together with fibroblast proliferation, presenting as firm, waxy, closely-set papules.
The condition spans a spectrum from a localised papular form, lichen myxoedematosus, to a generalised sclerodermoid form, scleromyxoedema, in which diffuse skin induration develops.
Scleromyxoedema produces characteristic signs including a leonine facial appearance and the doughnut sign, a raised rim around a central depression over the proximal interphalangeal joints.
The generalised form is almost always accompanied by a monoclonal gammopathy, most often an immunoglobulin G paraprotein with a lambda light chain.
Despite the name, it is not caused by thyroid disease and thyroid function is normal, which distinguishes it from the myxoedema of hypothyroidism.

Systemic involvement in scleromyxoedema may affect the nervous system, heart, gastrointestinal tract, muscles and joints, and the dermato-neuro syndrome of fever, seizures and coma is a feared complication.
Histology classically shows the triad of upper and mid-dermal mucin deposition, increased fibroblasts and fibrosis, best demonstrated with mucin stains such as Alcian blue.

Intravenous immunoglobulin is a favoured treatment for scleromyxoedema, with thalidomide, systemic corticosteroids, bortezomib, lenalidomide and autologous stem-cell transplantation used in resistant disease.
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder results from proliferation of dermal fibroblasts and their excessive production of glycosaminoglycans, predominantly hyaluronic acid, which accumulate in the upper and mid dermis and, in the generalised form, are accompanied by progressive dermal fibrosis. The consistent association of scleromyxoedema with a monoclonal gammopathy points to a pathogenic role for a circulating factor, and serum from affected patients has been shown to stimulate fibroblast proliferation, although the paraprotein itself does not appear to be directly responsible and its titre correlates poorly with disease activity. Pro-fibrotic and pro-inflammatory cytokines, including transforming growth factor beta, interleukin-1 and tumour necrosis factor, are implicated in driving the fibroblast response and matrix deposition. The mucin and fibrosis together produce the waxy papules and diffuse induration seen clinically, while extracutaneous mucin and vascular changes are thought to underlie the systemic manifestations, including the life-threatening dermato-neuro syndrome. Importantly the process is unrelated to the interstitial glycosaminoglycan accumulation of hypothyroid myxoedema, and the normal thyroid axis is a key point of distinction.
additionalDifferentials: Systemic sclerosis and other sclerodermoid disorders
Other primary cutaneous mucinoses such as reticular erythematous mucinosis
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with mucin stains such as Alcian blue or colloidal iron
Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation to detect a paraprotein
Bone marrow examination when a monoclonal protein is identified
Thyroid function tests to exclude hypothyroid myxoedema
Renal function and a gadolinium exposure history to exclude nephrogenic systemic fibrosis
Antinuclear and scleroderma-associated antibodies to exclude systemic sclerosis
redFlags: Neurological deterioration with fever, seizures or coma suggesting the dermato-neuro syndrome
Cardiac symptoms indicating myocardial or conduction involvement
Evidence of progression of the monoclonal gammopathy towards myeloma
Rapidly progressive skin induration limiting movement or respiration
reference.prognosis: Scleromyxoedema tends to run a chronic, progressive course and can be fatal, particularly if the dermato-neuro syndrome supervenes, although intravenous immunoglobulin has improved outcomes. The localised papular form lacks a paraprotein and systemic involvement and follows a benign, if persistent, course.
pitfalls: Confusing the condition with hypothyroid myxoedema on the basis of its name and overlooking the normal thyroid axis
Failing to investigate for and monitor an associated monoclonal gammopathy
Misdiagnosing the sclerodermoid form as systemic sclerosis
Overlooking systemic and neurological involvement in apparently skin-limited disease
Not excluding nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in a patient with renal impairment and gadolinium exposure
references: Clinical reviews of cutaneous mucinoses and scleromyxoedema
management: Intravenous immunoglobulin as first-line therapy for scleromyxoedema, which has improved outcomes

Additional systemic options for refractory disease including thalidomide or lenalidomide, systemic corticosteroids, plasma-cell-directed regimens such as bortezomib-based therapy, and autologous stem-cell transplantation
For the localised papular form of lichen myxoedematosus, observation or topical and intralesional corticosteroids, as it lacks systemic involvement
Monitoring of the associated monoclonal gammopathy with serum protein electrophoresis and surveillance for progression to myeloma
Urgent treatment of the dermato-neuro syndrome of fever, seizures and coma with intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange and corticosteroids
